newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia sees A$2 bln a year infrastructure leap.
newsitem.headline: Australia sees A$2 bln a year infrastructure leap.

text.p: Billions of dollars of Australian infrastructure projects are more likely to go ahead because of new works-boosting provisions in Australia's 1997/98 Federal budget, analysts and financiers told Reuters.

More than A$26 billion worth of projects which appeared to have been put on the shelf by the scrapping of an abuse-prone infrastructure bonds scheme in February are now seen as having received a new chance.
The provisions were announced in the 1997/98 budget unveiled on Tuesday.

But the more limited scope of Australia's new infrastructure deal, which involves tax rebates and possible infrastructure funding from a A$1 billion heritage fund, is of concern to some. "It's pretty good really," said Michael Price, executive director of project and structural finance at Macquarie Bank.

The new infrastructure rebate scheme and the possibility of a A$1 billion fund to mark the cententary of Australia's Federation in 1901 assisting infrastructure projects up to 2001 were both good steps, he said.

Projects which could be sparked into life by the rebate scheme, which is likely to finance up to A$2 billion a year in spending, range from the long-awaited 1,410 km Darwin-Alice Springs railway to other road and rail works.
But close observers, who not to be named, said the new scheme is considerably narrower than the scope of the axed infrastructure bonds scheme.

It provides only for private sector road and rail projects, as well as projects which had applied for infrastructure bonds at the Development Allowance Authority before the February 14 scrapping of infrastructure bonds.
"Energy, seaport, water, airport, gas pipelines, electricity, all miss out (apart from projects which had applied before)," one source said.
The new rebate scheme also caps the cost to government of A$75 million a year against A$200 million under the old scheme.

Treasury spokesman Rob Dalla-Costa agreed the rebate scheme was significantly narrowed from the old scheme, but also said there had been a real rush of projects onto the infrastructure bonds application queue before the February 14 cutoff.
All these projects were eligible under the new scheme, he said, adding he would not comment on specific projects.
While the rebate scheme made a lot of sense, the only issue was whether it would be adequate in size, Price said.
Hopefully if many deserving projects missed out because of the funding cap, they could be reassessed later, he said.
The infrastructure rebate scheme announced on Tuesday night sets a government funding cap of A$37.5 million for the first year, 1997/98, and A$75 million a year after that.
It is estimated to cost the government a total of A$262.5 million over the four years to 2000/01.

The government has not spelled out total infrastructure spending which would be allowed to proceed by the rebate, but the rate of rebate will be set at the lower of a financier's current year marginal tax rate or the 36 percent company tax.
The A$75 million cap would likely translate to about A$2 billion in annual borrowings for infrastructure spending, analysts and officials told Reuters.
"(That) is a fair bit, but there are a lot of private infrastructure projects which are around," Price said.
Asked which projects might go ahead, Price said "it's a bit early to tell". Other officials declined comment.
Clearly more than A$2 billion a year would dbe involved if road, rail and all projects which had applied for infrastructure bonds were taken together, Price said.
In this case the Australian Tax Office would work out which project received the benefit of the scheme, he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
